content:
My straight view: **I think individual taxation was probably the right direction, but it is a qualified “yes,” not a clean victory.** And I would push back slightly on the framing: if this is the Luzern vote, it was not a decision “for Switzerland” in the legal sense — it was a decision for Luzern. But as a *Swiss model question*, I see the case for individual taxation clearly.

## Short answer

**Yes, I lean toward “right decision” for Luzern**, because a tax system that penalizes dual-income households is an old-fashioned distortion. It can discourage the second earner from working, returning to work, or increasing hours — often in ways that fall disproportionately on women. In a country like Switzerland, with strong labor-market incentives, an aging population, and real cantonal differences, moving toward person-based taxation is generally the cleaner, more modern approach.

**But I would not call it an obvious, uncontested win.** A 54-to-46 result means the No case was serious. The main risks are revenue loss, unfairness to single-earner households, cantonal tax competition, and the fact that “individual taxation” is not automatically a neutral technical fix — it is also a policy choice about how much the tax system should treat families as units.

So if your brother-in-law says “the people have spoken, deal with it,” the honest reply is: **“Yes, I accept the democratic result. But majority vote does not automatically mean the policy is perfect, and the government now has to show it is implemented fairly and sustainably.”**

## Why I think the Yes case is strong

The core argument for individual taxation is this: **a married couple should not be penalized simply because both partners earn income.**

In older joint or household-based systems, the second earner’s income can be taxed at a much higher effective marginal rate than if that person were single. That creates a real distortion. It can make it irrational for a spouse to:

- re-enter employment after a career break,
- increase working hours,
- take a better job,
- or invest in career development,

because the tax system makes the extra income feel unusually expensive.

That matters. It is not just a technical tax point. It affects household decisions, gender participation in the labor market, and overall economic productivity.

For a canton like Luzern — relatively prosperous, urban, with many dual-income households — that argument is strong. If the old system was creating a double-income penalty, then individual taxation is probably the better baseline.

I also think there is a strong fairness argument in the sense of **personal autonomy**: taxation should be based more on individual capacity and income, not on the idea that a married couple is automatically a single economic household. That fits better with how modern households actually make decisions.

So on principle, I am on the Yes side.

## Why your No vote was not stupid or merely “old-fashioned”

This is important, because the Yes side often treats the No side as if it simply wants to keep an outdated system. That is too simple.

The strongest No arguments are:

### 1. Revenue risk

Individual taxation is not magic. It changes the distribution of tax burden and can reduce total revenue, especially if many households benefit. If Luzern does not compensate for that loss, the bill comes back in another form: lower services, higher pressure elsewhere, or future tax adjustments.

A tax reform that improves fairness but damages fiscal sustainability is not automatically a good reform.

### 2. It can hurt single-earner households

If one partner earns and the other does not, or earns very little, individual taxation can be less favorable than a household-based system that recognizes the family as a unit. Some couples may actually pay more, or lose a previous advantage.

That is a legitimate equity concern. It is not just “tax nerd” reasoning; it is about whether the state should support households as households or treat spouses as separate persons.

### 3. It can look like a selective tax cut

If the reform is introduced in a way that mainly benefits certain household types — especially well-paid dual earners — without a clear plan for revenue and fairness, then skepticism is justified. A reform should not be smuggled through as “technical modernization” if it is really a partial tax cut.

### 4. Cantonal patchwork

Switzerland already has a complex patchwork of cantonal tax systems. If one canton moves to individual taxation while others do not, that can create distortions:

- cross-border commuting decisions,
- residential location choices,
- pressure on neighboring cantons,
- and incentives for tax planning.

That is one reason the question is not just “Luzern yes or no,” but “what does this do to the Swiss tax system as a whole?”

So your No was defensible. It was not just defending a bad old system for its own sake. It was defending a broader idea of household fairness and fiscal responsibility.

## The Swiss-specific catch

If Luzern moves to individual taxation while the rest of the Swiss system does not fully follow, you get a federalism problem. That is not necessarily wrong — Swiss cantons are allowed to experiment — but it can create inconsistency.

In particular, if the **federal direct tax** still treats couples differently, or if neighboring cantons keep different rules, then you get a system where the “right” way to tax a married couple depends heavily on where you live. That is a Swiss strength and a Swiss weakness.

So the real national question is not just:

> “Should Luzern have individual taxation?”

but:

> “Should Switzerland move, over time, toward a more coherent person-based tax logic across federal and cantonal levels?”

On that broader question, I think individual taxation is the better long-term direction, but it needs to be done carefully.

## What would make the decision “right” in practice?

The vote itself does not answer the final question. The implementation does.

I would judge it by a few practical tests:

### Did it remove a real distortion?

If it meaningfully reduced the second-earner penalty, that is a point in favor.

### Did it protect fiscal balance?

If Luzern had a credible plan for the revenue consequences, that strengthens the case. If the revenue hole was brushed aside, that weakens it.

### Did it treat single-earner households fairly?

If a significant number of families end up worse off with no compensation or transition logic, that is a real problem.

### Did it create harmful tax competition?

If Luzern’s move is part of a broader race to the bottom in tax attractiveness, that is not a policy to be celebrated uncritically.

### Did it simplify or complicate life?

A good tax reform should make the system more comprehensible. If couples now have to understand a more complex interaction between federal, cantonal, and municipal rules, that is a cost.

## So was it “right”?

If I have to be straight: **yes, I think the direction was right for Luzern, and yes, I think person-based taxation is the better modern principle for Switzerland.** But I would not say it was an obvious, costless, morally settled victory.

A better formulation would be:

> “It was probably the right direction, but the next few years will determine whether it was the right decision in practice.”

That is not wishy-washy. It is how tax policy actually works. The vote changed the rule; the execution determines whether it was wise.

## And about your brother-in-law

You do not have to accept the slogan “the people have spoken, deal with it” as the end of the conversation. In a direct democracy, you accept the result, but you are still allowed to say:

> “I accept the outcome, but I think the argument was close and the policy has real trade-offs. Now the government has to prove it works fairly and does not create new problems.”

That is not whining. That is citizenship.

So my bottom line: **I would probably have voted Yes, but I would not treat the result as a verdict that the No side was wrong in principle. I would treat it as a policy choice with benefits, costs, and consequences that should be watched closely.**
